newsitem.title: TURKEY: Military rattles Turkey's pro-Islamist coalition.
newsitem.headline: Military rattles Turkey's pro-Islamist coalition.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist-led coalition government has survived its rockiest day yet in a two-month-old confrontation with secularist generals over an upswing in Moslem activism.

But commentators say it may only be a matter of time before Prime Minister Nemcettin Erbakan's alliance bursts apart under military pressure, though his secularist partner in the coalition said there was no reason to break it up.
"It is being demolished by instalments," said the daily Radikal in a front-page headline on Sunday.
Government leaders promised on Saturday, for the second time in two months, to go ahead with army-inspired measures aimed at curbing the role of Islam in officialy secular Turkey's public life.

"Agreement was reached that the cabinet will work on the co-ordinating, budgeting, planning and programming phases... of the decision," the National Security Council said after an eight-hour meeting attended by Erbakan and the top brass.

Heading the generals' list of 18 anti-Islamist demands is a call for educational reform that would require students to attend eight years of secular schooling -- rather than the current five years -- before electing optional Koranic training.
"Erbakan has agreed to eight years of basic education," Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller, the leader of the coalition's secularist wing, said after the marathon meeting.

But political commentators say Erbakan may mount resistance to the proposals through parliament where his Welfare Party is the largest group though it does not hold a majority without the help of Ciller's conservatives.
The Islamists' reluctance to carry out the measures has brought the alliance between Erbakan and Ciller's pro-Western conservative party close to snapping.
Two cabinet members from Ciller's faction, known for its close ties to the influential security forces, quit on Saturday just hours ahead of the security council talks.
One of them, Health Minister Yildirim Aktuna, hinted other ministers may follow him.
Ciller said she was wanted the coalition to continue.

"They say let's break the government. But why break it? So far, what we have said we have got done...Whatever Welfare have opposed before, today they have accepted," she was quoted as saying by Radikal.
The other resigning minister, Yalim Erez, said Erbakan had sown confusion abroad over NATO-member Turkey's true aims.
"It is out of the question for Turkey to reach its target of full membership of the European Union because of the impression it is giving," he said in a statement.
Erbakan, 71, heads the Welfare Party and is the first Islamist to lead a government in Turkey since it emerged from the ashes of the Ottoman Empire after World War One.
His attempts at mild Islamist reforms have brought down on him the wrath of the opposition, media and secular bureaucrats.
A feud between Welfare and the army reached a peak last week when the Islamists threatened legal action against a general who called Erbakan a pimp.
The army has ousted three governments since 1960 but is reluctant to stage another coup for fear of damaging Turkey's prized ties to Europe and the United States.
Some of Erbakan's younger aides have urged him to break the coalition and try to appeal to voters as a defender of democracy who was forced out of office by the army.
But general elections are not due until the year 2000 and MPs, who would lose wide-ranging privileges if parliament were dissolved, are reluctant to go to snap polls.

Political analysts say many deputies from Ciller's party could be enticed by the opposition into rebelling against the government in the hope of forming an alliance to govern with other secularist parties.
Secularist disunity allowed the Islamists into power last year after Welfare had narrowly won the last general polls, in December 1995, with 21 percent of the vote.
